A.a: You still put on a jacket, even with nothing on the calendar.
A.b: You do not own a jacket that isn't for weather.

A.a: Your ideal shoe collection tilts toward oxfords and derbies.
A.b: Your ideal shoe collection tilts toward sneakers and boots.

A.a: At a backyard barbecue, you're the one in a linen sport coat.
A.b: At a backyard barbecue, you're the one in a well-worn t-shirt.

A.a: Weddings are a chance to break out the good suit.
A.b: Weddings are an occasion to buy nothing you don't already own.

A.a: The necktie is a small daily ritual for you.
A.b: The necktie is a funeral-and-court-date-only proposition.

A.a: A free Saturday means a proper haircut and looking presentable running errands.
A.b: A free Saturday means not being seen by anyone who matters.

A.a: The phrase “dress code” is reassuring — someone else made the decision.
A.b: The phrase “dress code” makes you faintly claustrophobic.

A.a: Your imagined commute happens in trousers with a crease.
A.b: Your imagined commute happens in something you could also sleep in.

A.a: You'd rather be slightly overdressed than ever underdressed.
A.b: You'd rather be comfortable than risk overdressing for even a minute.

A.a: Your suitcase always contains at least one blazer, just in case.
A.b: Your suitcase contains nothing that needs hanging up.

A.a: Your ideal dinner reservation is the kind of place that assumes a jacket.
A.b: Your ideal dinner reservation has a line and no host stand.

A.a: Picture “getting dressed” and you see a shirt with a real collar.
A.b: Picture “getting dressed” and you see a hoodie.

A.a: Cufflinks and pocket squares are small pleasures you look for excuses to use.
A.b: Cufflinks and pocket squares are props from a costume department.

A.a: If your job vanished tomorrow, your wardrobe would barely need to change.
A.b: If your job vanished tomorrow, your wardrobe would become almost entirely different.

A.a: At a party full of strangers, you'd rather wait for the host to introduce you properly.
A.b: At a party full of strangers, you'd rather find your own way in within five minutes.

A.a: You'd rather arrive at a gathering exactly on time, maybe a touch early.
A.b: You'd rather arrive whenever, fashionably or otherwise late.

A.a: In an unfamiliar social setting, your instinct is to observe the room's norms and match them.
A.b: In an unfamiliar social setting, your instinct is to do your own thing and let the room adjust.

A.a: You think most occasions deserve a bit more ceremony than people give them.
A.b: You think most occasions would be better with a little less ceremony.

B.a: A jacket should hold its shape without you in it.
B.b: A jacket should move like it forgot it was a jacket.

B.a: You like a shoulder built up, a little like armor.
B.b: You like a shoulder barely there — natural, soft, unpadded.
You iron under duress, if at all.

B.a: Your favorite fabric behavior is crisp — you can hear it move.
B.b: Your favorite fabric behavior is soft — it's already broken in.

B.a: A trouser should break cleanly and hold a line.
B.b: A trouser should puddle a little at the ankle.

B.a: Starch is an old and useful friend.
You prefer a shirt collar that stands up on its own.
B.b: You prefer a shirt collar that rolls and folds with some life in it.

B.a: Given a choice of suiting, you'd take a sharp, fused, city suit.
B.b: Given a choice of suiting, you'd take an unlined jacket you could fold into a bag.

B.a: Your ideal knit is fully fashioned and precise.
B.b: Your ideal knit is slouchy, oversized, cocoon-like.

B.a: A crease down the front of a trouser leg is non-negotiable.
B.b: A crease down the front of a trouser leg never occurred to you.

B.a: A garment should look best on the hanger, before anyone's worn it.
B.b: A garment should look best on the body, after a full day of living in it.

B.a: “Well-made” means precision — every seam accounted for.
When packing, you fold everything into crisp rectangles.
B.b: When packing, you roll it all and hope for the best.

B.a: A blazer with no lining strikes you as unfinished.
B.b: A blazer with no lining is the only kind worth owning in summer.

B.a: Your ideal workday runs on a set schedule you rarely deviate from.
B.b: Your ideal workday has open blocks you fill as the day suggests.

B.a: Your to-do list is ordered, and you work it in sequence.
B.b: Your to-do list is a loose pile you get to eventually.

B.a: Assembling something new, you read the instructions start to finish first.
B.b: Assembling something new, you start building and check the manual only when stuck.

B.a: Under pressure, you become more procedural and by-the-book.
B.b: Under pressure, you become more improvisational.

C.a: Your closet, viewed from across the room, reads as a small riot of color.
C.b: Your closet, viewed from across the room, reads as a study in one or two tones.

C.a: Shown a bolt of loud plaid, you ask how much.
C.b: Shown a bolt of loud plaid, you ask them to put it away.

C.a: Socks, for you, are an opportunity.
C.b: Socks, for you, are a place to be quiet.

C.a: Your ideal shirt has a story — checks, stripes, or better.
C.b: Your ideal shirt is solid, or as close to it as possible.

C.a: You've been fondly described as “a lot.”
A pink or lavender jacket sounds like a Tuesday.
C.b: A pink or lavender jacket sounds like a costume.

C.a: Your favorite color to wear is whichever one no one else is wearing that day.
C.b: Your favorite color to wear is navy, grey, or something you already own six of.

C.a: You'd rather your outfit be noticed for its color.
C.b: You'd rather your outfit be noticed for its cut.

C.a: Mixing stripes with checks feels like a fun problem to solve.
C.b: Mixing stripes with checks feels like tempting fate.

C.a: Your ideal pocket square clashes on purpose.
C.b: Your ideal pocket square matches so quietly no one clocks it.

C.a: If your wardrobe were punctuation, it would be an exclamation point.
C.b: If your wardrobe were punctuation, it would be a period.

C.a: You'd sooner wear a bold check no one else would try.
C.b: You'd sooner wear a plain grey you could take anywhere.

C.a: Your jewelry and watches lean toward statement.
C.b: Your jewelry and watches lean toward barely there.

C.a: Given an identical coat in camel or cobalt, you take the cobalt.
C.b: Given an identical coat in camel or cobalt, you take the camel.

C.a: In a group photo, you're the one doing something memorable in it.
C.b: In a group photo, you're the one making sure everyone else looks good.

C.a: Given the chance to speak in front of a room, you'd take it even if you weren't asked.
C.b: Given the chance to speak in front of a room, you'd rather avoid it, even if you're capable.

C.a: At karaoke, you pick the song that gets the whole room's attention.
C.b: At karaoke, you sing something safe and hand off the mic.

C.a: You'd rather be the friend who tells the story everyone repeats later.
C.b: You'd rather be the friend who quietly holds the group together.

D.a: “No brown in town” strikes you as worth keeping.
D.b: “No brown in town” strikes you as adorable, in a museum-piece sort of way.

D.a: You'd rather your clothes look like they could've been worn, unaltered, sixty years ago.
D.b: You'd rather your clothes look like they couldn't have existed until this year.

D.a: Your favorite menswear reference is an old photograph of someone's grandfather.
D.b: Your favorite menswear reference is a runway show that confused half the room.

D.a: When a brand “reinterprets a classic,” your instinct is suspicion — leave it alone.
D.b: When a brand “reinterprets a classic,” your instinct is interest — show me.

D.a: A suit with no clear lapel strikes you as a solved problem, unsolved again.
D.b: A suit with no clear lapel strikes you as the only interesting question left.

D.a: You buy clothes expecting to wear them for decades, ideally passed down.
D.b: You buy clothes expecting to wear them until the idea they're chasing moves on.

D.a: Asymmetry in a garment feels like a mistake at the factory.
D.b: Asymmetry in a garment feels like the whole point.

D.a: Your ideal designer reveres the archive.
D.b: Your ideal designer wants to burn it down.

D.a: “Timeless” is a compliment that makes you feel understood.
D.b: “Timeless” is a compliment that makes you feel a little bored.

D.a: You're drawn to a garment's provenance — who made this, and how long ago.
D.b: You're drawn to a garment's concept — what is this trying to say.

D.a: A worn family heirloom watch beats a conceptual new release, every time.
D.b: It's close, but the conceptual new release usually wins.

D.a: You think fashion mostly moves in slow, respectful circles back to itself.
D.b: You think fashion mostly moves forward, whether anyone's ready or not.

D.a: Your ideal tailor has made the same three things beautifully for forty years.
D.b: Your ideal tailor is still figuring out what a jacket could be.

D.a: Family traditions and rituals are things you protect and keep exactly as they were.
D.b: Family traditions and rituals are things you feel free to update or drop.

D.a: Inheriting an old method, your instinct is to preserve how it's always been done.
D.b: Inheriting an old method, your instinct is to look for what needs to change.

D.a: You trust an idea more once it's survived a long time.
D.b: You trust an idea more when it hasn't been tried yet.

D.a: Nostalgia is a comfort you return to often.
D.b: Nostalgia is a trap you try to avoid.

E.a: A garment's first job is to survive whatever you're about to do in it.
E.b: A garment's first job is to look right doing very little.

E.a: You'd rather a jacket have four real pockets you actually use.
E.b: You'd rather a jacket have one good pocket and a beautiful line.

E.a: Given a choice of boots, you pick the ones built for a job site.
E.b: Given a choice of boots, you pick the ones built for a room with good lighting.

E.a: Waterproofing and abrasion resistance genuinely interest you.
E.b: Waterproofing and abrasion resistance are someone else's problem.

E.a: Your ideal outerwear has survived actual weather.
E.b: Your ideal outerwear has survived only the dry cleaner.

E.a: A tag that says “Cordura” or “ripstop” makes you lean in.
E.b: A tag that says “Cordura” or “ripstop” makes you glaze over.

E.a: You'd rather spend on a coat that outlasts a decade of winters.
E.b: You'd rather spend on a coat that photographs beautifully once.

E.a: Your pockets, right now, could hold a multitool.
E.b: Your pockets, right now, could hold a folded pocket square, at most.

E.a: A garment's beauty mostly comes from how well it does its job.
E.b: A garment's beauty mostly comes from how little it needs to do.

E.a: Given the choice, your fabric has real abrasion resistance.
E.b: Given the choice, your fabric drapes beautifully.

E.a: You think about your clothes in terms of what they're for.
E.b: You think about your clothes in terms of what they say.

E.a: A missing button matters only if it stops the garment working.
E.b: A missing button matters immediately, aesthetically, before anything else.

E.a: The best compliment for a jacket is “that thing's been everywhere with you.”
E.b: The best compliment for a jacket is “where did you find that.”

E.a: You'd rather your wardrobe be reviewed by a gear tester.
E.b: You'd rather your wardrobe be reviewed by a critic.

E.a: Given a problem, you first ask what actually needs to happen.
E.b: Given a problem, you first ask what the ideal version of this would look like.

E.a: You're more likely to keep something because it still works.
E.b: You're more likely to keep something because it still means something.

E.a: A gift that thrills you is something useful you needed anyway.
E.b: A gift that thrills you is something beautiful you'd never have bought yourself.

E.a: When something breaks, you fix it yourself if at all possible.
E.b: When something breaks, you find someone who can restore it properly.

F.a: Given unlimited money for one garment, you'd fly to a small atelier in Naples.
F.b: Given unlimited money for one garment, you'd fly to a denim mill in North Carolina.

F.a: Your ideal Sunday reading is about the history of Savile Row.
F.b: Your ideal Sunday reading is about the history of Levi's or Filson.

F.a: A jacket that fits “like a shirt” — soft, close, unstructured — sounds correct.
F.b: A jacket that fits “like a shirt” — soft, close, unstructured — sounds unfinished.

F.a: You're more drawn to the word “sprezzatura.”
F.b: You're more drawn to the word “rugged.”

F.a: Shopping for clothes, you'd want an espresso standing at the counter.
F.b: Shopping for clothes, you'd want a coffee to go, on the way somewhere.

F.a: Your mental image of “well-dressed” is set in a piazza.
F.b: Your mental image of “well-dressed” is set in a hardware store, somehow.

F.a: You'd rather your trousers were cut in Rome.
F.b: You'd rather your trousers were cut in a Midwest factory, the same way since 1960.

F.a: A brand's founding story appeals more when it involves generations of a tailoring family.
F.b: A brand's founding story appeals more when it involves a guy who needed pants that wouldn't rip.

F.a: A frayed buttonhole suggests an old-world hand actually sewed this.
F.b: A frayed buttonhole suggests you should've bought the tougher version.

F.a: Your ideal shoe was hand-lasted in a small workshop abroad.
F.b: Your ideal shoe was built to be resoled forever by the original American maker.

F.a: You imagine the perfect tailor speaking with an accent you can't quite place.
F.b: You imagine the perfect tailor speaking the same plainspoken way you do.

F.a: An appealing garment description reads “cut with an unstructured shoulder, Neapolitan tradition.”
F.b: An appealing garment description reads “built tough, made to be worked in, guaranteed for life.”

F.a: Your style influences trace back to European film — a well-dressed man in a Fellini frame.
F.b: Your style influences trace back to American work — a rancher, a machinist, a ballplayer between games.

F.a: Given an heirloom to inherit, you'd take a grandfather's bespoke overcoat from Rome.
F.b: Given an heirloom to inherit, you'd take a grandfather's toolbox and the jacket he wore to use it.

F.a: Free in a new city, you'd find the oldest café in town and sit for two hours.
F.b: Free in a new city, you'd find whoever's doing something interesting and join in.

F.a: Talking about your work, you're more likely to describe the philosophy behind it.
F.b: Talking about your work, you're more likely to describe what you actually built.

F.a: You're more drawn to stories about old-world craftsmen who've done one thing for fifty years.
F.b: You're more drawn to stories about self-made people who figured it out themselves.

F.a: Given a choice of mentor, you'd pick someone steeped in tradition and formal training.
F.b: Given a choice of mentor, you'd pick someone who learned everything the hard way, on the job.

G.a: Cowboy boots and a big belt buckle feel like Tuesday.
G.b: Cowboy boots and a big belt buckle feel like a costume outside a rodeo.

G.a: You'd rather your view out the window be a mountain range.
G.b: You'd rather your view out the window be a skyline.

G.a: A pickup truck makes more sense to you than a subway map.
G.b: A subway map makes more sense to you than a pickup truck.

G.a: Your ideal Saturday involves a horse, a boat, or at least a very large dog.
G.b: Your ideal Saturday involves a gallery opening and a dinner reservation.

G.a: You feel more like yourself standing in an empty field than a crowded sidewalk.
G.b: You feel more like yourself standing on a crowded sidewalk than an empty field.

G.a: You know how to fix a fence, start a fire, or back up a trailer.
G.b: You know how to hail a cab in the rain and navigate a subway transfer without looking at your phone.

G.a: Silence and distance sound like luxury to you.
G.b: Noise and proximity sound like luxury to you.

G.a: You'd rather your nearest neighbor be a mile away.
G.b: You'd rather your nearest neighbor be on the other side of a shared wall.

G.a: A big truck or a work vehicle appeals to you more than public transit ever will.
G.b: Not owning a car sounds like freedom, not inconvenience.

G.a: You dress with the expectation that you might need to get your boots muddy.
G.b: You dress with the expectation that the ground beneath you is pavement.

G.a: Your ideal hometown has one traffic light, maybe two.
G.b: Your ideal hometown has too many people to ever fully know.

G.a: A big sky and open land make you feel calm.
G.b: A packed calendar and a full street make you feel alive.

G.a: You'd rather learn to ride, hunt, or fish than learn to navigate a subway system in a new city.
G.b: You'd rather learn to navigate a subway system in a new city than learn to ride, hunt, or fish.

G.a: You measure distance in hours driven, without much complaint.
G.b: You measure distance in blocks, and complain if it's more than ten.

G.a: A flannel shirt, to you, is just a shirt.
G.b: A flannel shirt, to you, is a look you'd put on for a specific mood.

G.a: You'd rather your Friday night end around a fire outside.
G.b: You'd rather your Friday night end at a bar with a line outside.

G.a: You trust a place more once you've seen its weather do something extreme.
G.b: You trust a place more once you've found the best coffee within walking distance.

G.a: Given the choice, your closet should survive a barn.
G.b: Given the choice, your closet should survive a crowded elevator at rush hour.
